Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) shares are up 7.43% in today's regular session, trading at $198.96 as of 1:15 PM ET. The catalyst came late Thursday, Nov. 5, when Lam Research announced a new $25 billion buyback authorization. The announcement followed a sharp selloff in semiconductor stocks, as Benzinga reported. Sundry Photography / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

Lam makes the equipment chipmakers use to manufacture semiconductors, including deposition, etch, and clean tools. A buyback authorization lets the company repurchase its own shares over time. It does not require Lam to buy any shares, and the program can be suspended. Before this announcement, Lam had $3 billion remaining under its prior authorization at the end of the September quarter. The long-term goal is still to return 85% of free cash flow to shareholders.

Today's gain comes after a steep fall. Lam shares are down 21.79% over the past week and 40.41% over the past month. One session of buying is not a trend reversal.

title: Michael Burry Takes Profits on Major AI Bear Bet

Michael Burry (Trades, Portfolio) has started taking profits on one of his biggest bearish technology bets.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with NVDA.

Is NVDA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

NVDA GF Value chart

The famed investor disclosed that he sold 25% of his put options on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) after a sharp selloff across U.S. chip and technology stocks.

But that does not mean Burry has turned bullish.

He said the remaining SMH put position has become very large, suggesting the trade still represents a major part of his bearish exposure.

That distinction matters because SMH owns many of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, including Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE:TSM), AMD (NASDAQ:AMD), Broadcom and Micron (NASDAQ:MU).

The timing also makes sense.

SMH plunged about 11.2% on November 5, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% and the QQQ ETF dropped 6.5%, giving bearish positions a significant opportunity to lock in gains.

Burry had previously concentrated much of his bearish exposure into puts on SMH and the Nasdaq-100 with expirations in 2027, while arguing that the AI trade could be approaching a major market top.

He is also still holding puts on Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR), Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), Caterpillar and QQQ, according to his latest disclosure.

At the same time, Burry is not broadly bearish on every stock.

He disclosed that he added to his position in MercadoLibre, buying shares below $1,500 after the company reported earnings.

Investor Takeaway

I think the key point is that Burry is trimming risk, not reversing his thesis.

Selling 25% of the SMH puts after an 11% one-day plunge is classic profit-taking.

The more important signal is that he still describes the remaining position as very large and continues to hold several other bearish technology bets.

That means investors should not read this as Burry calling a bottom in semiconductors.

Instead, it suggests he believes the selloff has already moved far enough to justify locking in some gains while still expecting further downside.

For investors, the key things to watch are whether Burry trims more of the position, Nvidia's next earnings report, semiconductor valuations, AI capex expectations, and whether the broader Nasdaq correction deepens from here.

He is taking some money off the table.

He is not leaving the trade.

title: How Quant Strategies and Leveraged ETFs Helped Fuel Thursday's QQQ Bloodbath on Wall Street — and Whether It's Safe to Buy Yet
detail:
How Quant Strategies and Leveraged ETFs Helped Fuel Thursday's QQQ Bloodbath on Wall Street — and Whether It's Safe to Buy Yet
Sarah Holzmann
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 6:47 AM MST 3 min read
QQQ
Trade QQQ on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) cratered over 6% on Thursday in its worst single-session loss since March 2020, erasing approximately $2.3 trillion in market value and driving the Nasdaq-100 Index ($IUXX) firmly into correction territory at nearly 15% below its October 6 record high.

The headline damage was staggering, but the buried number that may matter more for months to come is UBS's estimate that roughly 30% of expected 2028 U.S. data center capacity additions are now at risk from construction pauses and regulatory headwinds — a figure large enough to invalidate forward earnings estimates across the semiconductor and cloud infrastructure complex.

More News from Barchart

Dear Tesla Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 29

Why It's Time to Buy the Pullback in Dell Stock

Dear Rocket Lab Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 9

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

How the Blue Wave Spiraled for AI Stocks

The selloff was ostensibly triggered by a sharp reassessment of the AI infrastructure buildout following the Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress and key governorships, including Texas, where the incoming governor has advocated an immediate moratorium on new data center construction. That policy threat transforms what had been a consensus long trade — leveraged bets on hyperscaler capital expenditure projected near $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027 — into a binary political risk.

However, the reaction to that headline was wildly amplified by massive selling on the part of systematic quant strategies, according to JPMorgan analysts.

Momentum Unwind Amplified the Carnage

Early in Thursday's session, momentum-chasing algorithms were forced to unwind concentrated long positions in the same AI and chip names that had led the market higher for months. Smaller multi-strategy hedge funds reportedly blew out positions en masse, while long-only institutional buyers refused to step in, creating what market participants characterized as a buyer's strike.

JPMorgan's team reports that leveraged ETFs unwound stock exposures in excess of $60 billion by the close, and 90% of that selling was focused in tech.

Retail investors compounded the dynamic by dumping a net $338 million in individual stocks in a single day — the largest single-session retail outflow since the COVID crash.

History Tilts Cautiously Constructive, But Beware

The evidence for buying the dip is mixed but not dismissive: the Nasdaq Composite ($NASX) has averaged a 21% return in the 12 months following its first close in correction territory across 10 instances in the past decade, and post-midterm six-month returns for the S&P 500 Index ($SPX) have averaged 15% since 1950.

title: This Chip CEO Just Warned the Data Center Market Is in a 'Bubble.' Which Stocks Are Most Exposed?
detail:
This Chip CEO Just Warned the Data Center Market Is in a 'Bubble.' Which Stocks Are Most Exposed?
Jonathan Ponciano, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 7:40 AM MST 4 min read
MCHP
NVDA
QQQ
SMH
^NDX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Plenty of investors have wondered whether the artificial intelligence boom has gone too far. On Thursday, the head of a $35 billion chipmaker effectively said so directly.

"I have been saying it, that data center is in the bubble," Steve Sanghi, president and CEO of Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP), said on the company's earnings call Thursday evening, according to a recording of the call.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The timing was hard to miss. Earlier that day, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, fell 6.5%, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) dropped 11.2%. Microchip itself tumbled 13.9% during the session, before it reported results after the closing bell. (Shares are up less than 1% in pre-market trading on Friday.)

Image source: Getty Images.

What He Actually Said

Sanghi's warning came in response to an analyst's question about whether an AI slowdown could spill over into Microchip's other markets, such as industrial and aerospace customers.

His answer was simply no. He said data centers account for 16.7% of Microchip's business, and he argued that much of the "upside and bubble is not in our numbers. It is in everybody else's numbers." If data-center spending were to correct, he said, Microchip "should outperform" companies that sell mostly into that market.

He also pointed to a newer risk: politics, which is what had much of the market reeling post-midterm elections. He said Microchip can't always tell whether its customers' chips are headed into an existing data center "or are they shipping in a data center in Ohio that the local governor is going to put on hold?"

Which Stocks Are Most Exposed

If Sanghi is right, the companies with the most to lose are the ones whose growth depends almost entirely on data-center construction. For example, equipment and construction companies sell into new projects, so a pause in building hits them first and hardest, but others are also exposed.

Several firms have already been hit hard. From Tuesday's close through Thursday's:

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) fell 12%. Data centers brought in $89 billion of its $96.2 billion in revenue during the second quarter, or about 92%, according to its most recent quarterly filing. Third-quarter earnings are due later this month.

Vertiv (NYSE:VRT), which makes the power and cooling equipment inside data centers, fell 25%.

Comfort Systems USA (NYSE:FIX), a contractor that builds mechanical and electrical systems for these sites, also fell 25%.

Ciena (NYSE:CIEN), which makes optical-networking gear that moves data between facilities, fell 23%.

Applied Digital (NASDAQ:APLD), which builds and leases data centers for AI customers, fell 20%.
